beats.text: They made him a cook. Then Pearl Harbor.

overlays.hook: They made him a cook. *Then Pearl Harbor.*

beats.text: In 1939, this Texas farm boy joined the Navy, where Black sailors were kept to feeding and serving the officers.
On December 7, 1941, he was collecting laundry on the battleship West Virginia when the torpedoes hit.

visual.caption: USS West Virginia, Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941

beats.text: His battle station was destroyed. So he helped carry the wounded.
Then he took a fifty-caliber machine gun he had never been trained to use, and fired at the planes until the ammunition ran out.
Later he said, I just pulled the trigger, and she worked fine.
The Navy praised him without giving his name. A Black newspaper found it.

visual.caption: Pearl Harbor, seen from a Japanese plane

beats.text: In May 1942, Admiral Nimitz pinned on the Navy Cross. He was the first Black sailor to receive it.

visual.caption: Admiral Nimitz and Doris Miller, 27 May 1942

beats.text: But his job did not change. The hero was still a mess attendant.
In 1943, a Japanese submarine sank his ship, the Liscome Bay. He was twenty-four.
They gave him a tray. He picked up a gun.
Follow The Black History Room for more.

facts.claim: Enlisted Sept 1939; Black recruits largely restricted to the messman branch.
Collecting laundry on USS West Virginia when torpedoes hit, 7 Dec 1941.
Station destroyed; helped wounded and moved Capt. Bennion.
.50-caliber machine gun with no training on it.
"I just pulled the trigger, and she worked fine."
Navy commendation 1 Jan 1942 unnamed; Pittsburgh Courier identified him, March 1942.
Navy Cross from Nimitz 27 May 1942; first Black recipient.
Cook third class; lost on Liscome Bay 24 Nov 1943, aged 24.

notUsed: CVN-81 left out of the reel: its name is in question in 2026 reports; the long video covers it.
